content: 1. Prolonged use of vancomycin can lead to the overgrowth of microorganisms that are not susceptible to the drug. Patients should be carefully monitored during treatment. If a superinfection occurs, appropriate measures must be taken. 2. Rarely, pseudomembranous colitis caused by Clostridioides difficile has been reported in patients receiving intravenous vancomycin. 3. To reduce the risk of nephrotoxicity in patients with pre-existing renal dysfunction or those receiving concurrent aminoglycoside therapy, renal function should be monitored regularly, and dosing schedules should be carefully followed. 4. Serial auditory function tests may help minimize the risk of ototoxicity. 5. Reversible neutropenia has been reported in patients receiving vancomycin. Patients undergoing prolonged therapy or those on concomitant drugs that may cause neutropenia should have their leukocyte counts monitored periodically. 6. Vancomycin is irritating to tissues and must be administered via a secure intravenous route. Accidental extravasation can cause pain, tenderness, and tissue necrosis. Thrombophlebitis may occur, but its frequency and severity can be reduced by slow infusion and rotating venous access sites. 7. Infusion-related events, such as hypotension, flushing, erythema, urticaria, and pruritus, are more common when vancomycin is administered with anesthetic agents. These events can be minimized by infusing vancomycin over 60 minutes before anesthetic induction. 8. The safety and efficacy of vancomycin administered intrathecally (via intralumbar or intraventricular routes) or intraperitoneally have not been established in well-controlled trials. Intraperitoneal administration during continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) has been associated with chemical peritonitis, which typically resolves after discontinuation of intraperitoneal vancomycin. 9. Prescribing vancomycin without a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial infection or prophylactic indication is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. 10. Concurrent or sequential use of vancomycin with other potentially neurotoxic or nephrotoxic drugs, such as amphotericin B, aminoglycosides, bacitracin, polymyxin B, colistin, viomycin, or cisplatin, requires careful monitoring. 11. Animal reproduction studies have not been conducted with vancomycin, and its effects on reproductive capacity are unknown. In a controlled clinical study, vancomycin was found in cord blood when administered to pregnant women for serious staphylococcal infections. No sensorineural hearing loss or nephrotoxicity attributable to vancomycin was observed in infants, though one infant experienced conductive hearing loss unrelated to vancomycin. Due to limited data, it is unclear whether vancomycin causes fetal harm. It should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. 12. Vancomycin is excreted in human milk. Caution is advised when administering vancomycin to nursing mothers. A decision should be made to either discontinue nursing or discontinue the drug, considering its importance to the mother. 13. In pediatric patients, it may be necessary to confirm desired vancomycin serum concentrations. Concurrent administration of vancomycin with anesthetic agents has been associated with erythema and histamine-like flushing in pediatric patients. The potential for toxic effects from chemicals leaching from plastic containers into single-dose, premixed intravenous preparations has not been determined. 14. In elderly patients, the natural decline in glomerular filtration with age may lead to elevated vancomycin serum concentrations if dosage is not adjusted. Dosage schedules should be modified accordingly. 15. Patients should be informed that antibacterial drugs, including vancomycin, should only be used to treat bacterial infections. They should be advised to take the medication exactly as directed, even if they feel better early in the course of therapy. Skipping doses or not completing the full course of therapy may reduce the effectiveness of treatment and increase the likelihood of developing drug-resistant bacteria. 16. Diarrhea is a common side effect of antibiotics and usually resolves after discontinuation. However, patients should be aware that watery and bloody stools, with or without stomach cramps and fever, can occur even two or more months after completing antibiotic therapy. If this happens, they should contact their physician immediately.
